new_statements.quote: [Barrett 1996: 30] "In Mam, short unstressed vowels are usualy dropped before a stressed vowel (cf. England 1983, 43-4). Sipakapense has adopted this process of dropping vowels before stress (which generally falls on the last syllable of a word)." [Barrett 2002: 7] "Sipakapense (Barrett 1999), a Mayan language related to K'ichee', also has this type of stress system. Sipakapense has a very straight-forward stress system of quantity-insensitive R → L iambs [...] Examples of Sipakapense stress are given in 14) below: kuwìts'ulí 'Come hug him/her!' kùuwìts'ulí 'Come hug us' kàtktsulí 'They hugged you' katìntsulí 'I hugged you' atí 'man' iiáq 'woman' kiib'ék 'they are going'"

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Barrett 1996 (BLS 22, pp. 25-36): opened via the scanned text and the page image ocr_barrett1996/PDF p. 7 = printed p. 30; the PDF's p. 1 is a cover sheet, p. 2 is printed p. 25). Under the heading "3.2 Phonology" the image reads exactly: "In Mam, short unstressed vowels are usualy dropped before a stressed vowel (cf. England 1983, 43-4). Sipakapense has adopted this process of dropping vowels before stress (which generally falls on the last syllable of a word). Thus, many root vowels drop or surface depending on morphology:" -- verbatim, including the original's "usualy". The examples in (9) on the same page carry acute accents on the final syllable (iʃiím "corn", w+ʃím "my corn", ʃ+ø+in+b…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the word, regardless of syllable weight (vowel length does not attract stress). Feet are quantity-insensitive iambs built right-to-left, so in the 2002 transcription secondary stress lands on every second syllable counting leftward from the final one. Short vowels in the syllable before the stressed one are deleted, which is why Sipakapense words carry long consonant clusters.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Barrett 2002, example (14), marks secondary stress (grave accent) on alternating syllables leftward from the final primary stress (kùuwìts'ulí, kàtktsulí, katìntsulí), i.e. right-to-left iambic footing, and calls the system quantity-insensitive. Bennett 2016 (sec. 6.1.1) explicitly lists Barrett 1999, 2002 among impressionistic secondary-stress reports that 'should be treated with caution'.
new_statements.exceptions: Barrett 1996 hedges with 'generally'. Barrett 2002 (p. 7) says the iambic system arose by reanalysis of the K'ichee' system on roots with an even number of syllables. The ALMG Gramática normativa (2011) and Monografía (2007) mention 'certain non-standard words accented on the penultimate syllable' shared with Cunén K'iche' (Kunenteko), used only as historical evidence, without listing them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the 1996 statement is made while describing pre-tonic vowel syncope inside words (root vowels drop or surface depending on morphology); the 2002 examples are inflected verb forms and bare nouns (atí 'man', iiáq 'woman'). Nothing said about phrase-level or citation-form effects. Bennett 2016 (sec. 6.1) notes final stress is the K'ichean norm and that phrase-final prominence can be confused with word stress in the family.
new_statements.identity_note: Barrett's data are from the single Sipakapense-speaking community of Sipacapa, San Marcos (Glottolog sipa1247, no sub-dialects listed); older sources call the language Sipacapa / Sipacapeño / 'Quiche of Sipacapa' (Hoiland & Sánchez 1980). No identity problem.

sources.note: Sec. 6.1: 'Final stress (36a) is the norm in K'ichean languages'; sec. 6.1.1: reports of secondary stress incl. Barrett 1999, 2002 are impressionistic and 'should be treated with caution'. Sipakapense itself is cited (Barrett 1999, 2011; Tema Bautista 2005) only for pre-tonic vowel syncope and consonant clusters, no Sipakapense-specific stress statement.

sources.note: p. 7 (PDF p. 8): Sipakapense 'has a very straight-forward stress system of quantity-insensitive R -> L iambs'; example (14) shows final primary stress with alternating secondary stress leftward (kuwìts'ulí, kùuwìts'ulí, kàtktsulí, katìntsulí, atí, iiáq, kiib'ék); says the system is a reanalysis of the K'ichee' system based on roots with an even number of syllables.
